match.reason: Neither bank point teaches both halves of this point: mat-ratios covers only ratios (with sharing, which the brief does not mention), and mat-rates-conversions covers only rates and unit conversion, so a new point that defines the ratio-versus-rate distinction is the safer match.

draft.title: Ratios and rates
card: A ratio compares amounts of the same kind, in the same unit. A ratio of 2:3 means 2 parts to 3 parts.
A rate compares amounts in different units, such as km per hour or dollars per kilogram. To find a rate, divide by the amount of the second unit.

To share in a ratio, add the parts, then divide the total by that number to find one part. Example: share $40 in the ratio 1:3. Parts = 1 + 3 = 4, so one part = 40 ÷ 4 = $10. The shares are $10 and $30.
Rate example: 150 km in 3 hours is 150 ÷ 3 = 50 km per hour.
draft.remember: A ratio compares the same units. A rate compares different units.

a.q: Which of these is a rate?
opts: 3 red cups for every 5 blue cups
20 girls in a class of 30 students
A 4 m rope cut into 2 m pieces
a.why: Kilometres and hours are different units, so 240 km in 3 hours is a rate (80 km per hour). Red cups to blue cups compares the same kind of thing, so it is a ratio.

b.q: Liam and Ava share $350 in the ratio 3:4. How much does Ava get?
b.why: Parts = 3 + 4 = 7, so one part = 350 ÷ 7 = $50. Ava has 4 parts, so 4 × 50 = $200. Liam's share is $150, which is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Find the value of one part first.
